Macrons

SearchHow we decideRulings

Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

proud adjective

arrogant, thinking oneself above others

also arrogant, haughty, stuck-up, pride (arrogance)

classical

Plaut. Asin. 470: nōn decet superbum esse hominem servom
Cic. Att. 8.4.1: superbum sē praebuit

superbus, superba, superbum

adjective

proud, haughty, arrogant

The usual word, always in a bad sense in classical prose: one who thinks himself above others, and so rude and overbearing (Lewis & Short). The noun is superbia, pride. In poetry it can also be “proud of, splendid” (see proud, pleased).

Other words

  • arrogāns, arrogantis — arrogant, presumptuous

    adjective, third declension, one ending: the participle of arrogō, “claim for oneself” · also used · classical · Traupman 149: arrogāns, arrogant; arrogantia, arrogance

    One who claims more for himself than is his due.

  • īnsolēns, īnsolentis — arrogant, insolent; also unusual, unaccustomed

    adjective, third declension, one ending · also used · classical · Liv. 5.48.9: additus ab īnsolente Gallō ponderī gladius

    Its first sense is “unaccustomed, unusual” (verbum īnsolēns, an unusual word, Gell. 1.10.4); from there, behaving beyond what is customary: arrogant, overbearing, especially in success (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • Nimis īrācundē. nōn decet superbum esse hominem servom.

    Far too hot-tempered. It doesn’t suit a slave to be proud.Plaut. Asin. 470

  • tumēns inānī grāculus superbiā pennās pāvōnī quae dēciderant sustulit sēque exōrnāvit

    a jackdaw, swollen with empty pride, picked up the feathers that had fallen from a peacock and decked himself outPhaedr. 1.3.4–7

  • Contrītiōnem praecēdit superbia, et ante ruīnam exaltātur spīritus.

    Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.Vulg. Prov. 16.18

See also proud.

SourcesLewis & Short: superbus · Lewis & Short: arrogans · Lewis & Short: insolens
